## Active

### D-019 — blong-party demonstrates the profile feature too

> _2026-08-21 · realm/blong-party · active_

The blong-party app gained the blong-access browser child, the `profile` config and the
`integration` testHook block, plus a `partyTestProfileMerge` dbTest seed that links testAdmin to a
`party.person` row through `hasProfile`. Verified explicitly while doing it: the access browser
child, the profile config and the testHook on their own do NOT break google or self-registration —
only nesting `login`/`google` inside the inner `portal` did.

### D-347 — ACL matrix is a Gherkin DataTable asserted by a realm helper

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

ACL matrix test representation: a Gherkin DataTable inside one scenario, asserted by an ACL-specific
helper in blong-party. Column 1 is a box-drawing org tree whose leaf rows are the persons (viewers),
the remaining columns are the subject persons of a party.person.get probe, cells are the allowed
tick, the denied cross, the RBAC forbidden sign and a dot or blank for not-asserted, and a trailing
notes column carries the per-row explanation plus the grant summary on org and unit rows. One
scenario asserts every cell; the helper re-renders the tree and grid only when a cell mismatches.

### D-348 — ACL matrix probes through the HTTP gateway

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

The ACL matrix probes party.person.get through the HTTP gateway, not in-process, because the gateway
RBAC check is a Fastify preHandler: an in-process tap call bypasses it and a caller with no grant
receives acl.notFound instead of 403. The matrix therefore runs as a browser-side flow like
test$Object.flow, with party added to the test client backend proxied namespaces, and logs in as
each viewer before probing its row.

### D-349 — ACL matrix seed reuses the party and access merges

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

The ACL matrix fixture is two new meta/dbTest YAML seeds that reuse existing handlers:
party.hierarchy.merge for the orgs, units and persons, and access.authorization.merge for the users,
roles, scopes and rules. The filenames are prefixed so the party merge runs before the authorization
merge, and the fixture uses short names (Axis, Beta, Amy, Ben, ...) that do not touch the existing
Global Bank Corp and FinServe hierarchy.

### D-352 — The gateway-application ACL matrix lives in blong-party

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

The fourth matrix needed gateway applications as callers, so blong-party now lists
@feasibleone/blong-gateway as a devDependency and adds it as a server child (srv, login, core,
access, gateway, party), with gateway: {} in the party dev config. Rejected alternatives were
putting the matrix in blong-gateway (the aclMatrix helper and the Axis/Beta fixture live in
blong-party, so that duplicates both) and a new cross-realm test package (more moving parts for one
table). The cost of this choice is that blong-party's dev database now also carries the gateway
schema (gateway_application, gateway_bundle, gateway_subscription) and the suite loads one more
realm. Reverse it by moving browser/test/feature/aclMatrixApplication.ts and
browser/test/test/testAclMatrixApplication.ts and meta/dbTest/23- through 26- into blong-gateway and
copying the helper.

### D-353 — The application matrix's eight apps mirror its bundles one-to-one

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

One application per bundle, named after the scope it is subscribed to: axis-app, axis-hq-app,
north-app, south-app, beta-app, east-app, any-app (the wildcard-allow bundle) and none-app (no
subscription at all, so RBAC forbids every cell). All eight share the pinned secret testAppSecret
written by gateway.application.merge. The expectations were reasoned out and then corrected from the
first run: axis-hq-app reads the persons of Axis HQ and no unit record, because a unit's only scope
predicate is belongsTo.

### D-354 — Each ACL matrix asserts its fixture in a Background, one column per predicate

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

The four matrix features open with a Background of Data Tables (the org chart, the users, accounts
or applications, the grants, the rules) that the shared aclFixture library checks against the graph
through the new party.fixture.get read. Every column is one predicate (belongsTo, isPartOf, hasRole,
hasScope, hasCapability, plus clientId), so a cell is a claim about the seeded triples rather than a
comment, and a cell states every target of that subject and predicate - an edge the fixture does not
declare fails the table instead of passing unnoticed. The user chose declared triples over derived
authorization, and a Background over per-scenario repetition, so the tables are written once per
feature and checked before each scenario. Reversal is cheap: delete the Background blocks and the
aclFixture library, since the matrices do not depend on them.

### D-355 — Fixture usernames are the lower-case person name

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

A person and its user are two records (a party.person and an access.user) and nothing links them in
the graph, so the fixture names the user after its person in lower case: Amy the person, amy the
user. The seed keys in 21-aclMatrix-accessAuthorizationMerge.yaml became amy, ben, cam, dee, fay and
gil, and the aclMatrix helper signs a password viewer in as its label lower-cased, with a usernames
map to override. The case is the link, and it is what makes the two namespaces readable side by side
in the fixture tables. Reversal: restore the capitalised keys and pass the map.

### D-356 — The fixture read is a new dbTest handler exposed by a gateway validation

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

party.fixture.get (realm/blong-party/adapter/dbTest/partyFixtureGet.ts) returns the fixture as named
facts, resources, rules and clientIds in four queries, and it needed a validation file
(realm/blong-party/gateway/party/partyFixtureGet.ts) to be reachable through the gateway at all. The
rejected alternative was reading the same data through the generic CRUD that already exists
(core.triple.find, core.resource.find, access.acl.find): those return binary ids rather than names,
so the helper would resolve every name to an id first and issue a call per predicate. The capability
matrixFixtureRead, granted to Admin, authorises it, and the handler is dev-only because the db
adapter loads .dbTest groups only under dev.

### D-358 — The matrix probes declare the refusals they expect

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

Every ACL matrix cell is a real call, so an expected refusal was logged as an error: 467 error-level
entries per green run of the party suite, 461 of them the cells doing what the feature file says.
The probes now pass expect on the call (acl.notFound and gateway.notAllowed for a matrix cell,
gateway.notAllowed alone for the fixture read, account.exists and gateway.notAllowed in the two
registration flows), and the suite's error stream is empty. The refusals are still thrown and still
asserted on; only the level changed. The declaration is per call rather than per suite on purpose,
since the same viewer may be expected to fail one cell and succeed on another.

### D-359 — The failure report is a contract with its own feature

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

A matrix is only worth its green run if a red one locates the failure, so the report is asserted
rather than assumed: both helpers render through one padded table renderer (exported from
aclMatrix.ts, used by aclFixture.ts), the offending cell reads expected not-equal actual, and every
mismatch is named with its row, column and both values. The contract is held by the feature
test.acl.diagnostics (browser/test/feature/aclDiagnostics.ts), which drives the real helpers with a
deliberately wrong table and asserts that each mismatch sits in the cell it belongs to, then that a
table with nothing wrong reports nothing. It was verified by mutating the marker, which fails that
feature. A unit test would not have covered the path a reader actually sees, which is why it is a
feature.

### D-360 — The matrices cover the unscoped hole with two records

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

The concept's decision matrix has a term the matrices did not show: verdict = unscoped ? ALLOW :
guarded. Two records now exist only for it. Hal is a person in no unit at all (no belongsTo edge),
so his column is allowed for every viewer that holds the read, the record deny that matrixNorth
names him with is ignored, and the wildcard deny of matrixDenyAll does not close it either. Ivy is a
person in North whose role is scoped like matrixAxis (Axis HQ) and carries a deny on every record,
so her row shows a deny beating a grant and her own record denied, with the hole left open on Hal.
Hal is a column and deliberately not a row: he has no user, and a row labelled like a column is a
viewer to the helper, which would sign in as a user that does not exist. The three cases pass
against the live graph, which is the concept's claim confirmed rather than restated.

### D-361 — The three remaining concept cases are deferred, not guessed

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

The named section's cases are covered and verified; three cases from the concept's verdict tables
are not, and I chose to defer them while the user was away rather than decide for them (T-197). mode
explicit needs a guarded table that exists nowhere in the repository, which changes blong-party's
schema and the concept's own statement that nothing declares the shape yet. add with addScope needs
a write matrix rather than a get probe, and the matrices are deliberately read-only today. mode none
needs records of an unguarded table in the fixture. Each also costs probes the suite can barely
afford (148 seconds of tap's 180, with the application matrix at 80), so any of them should come
with the trim T-196 asks for. Reversal is the same as the decision: pick one and implement it;
nothing in the four matrices depends on their absence.

### D-362 — The last three ACL cases: two matrices, no matrix for writes

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · active_

The concept's verdict tables listed three cases the matrices did not cover, and each got a different
treatment. The unguarded case is a matrix over access.acl, the rules table itself, because it is
seeded in this suite, has a model and declares no acl at all: its columns are the records the seeded
rules target, resolved by the joined targetName in code because a virtual name cannot be filtered.
The explicit case is a matrix over a new party.consent table in the party realm, declared mode
explicit with no scopes, which is what makes a scope rule match nothing and a record rule admit
exactly one row. The add and addScope case gets no matrix by the user's choice: a matrix probes a
record, so a write row would create one record per cell, and the in-process test.acl.flow already
drives party.person.add with a submitted belongsTo edge and asserts the scope the guard resolved.
The tap ceiling for a package was raised with it, from 180s to 240s: an ACL matrix signs in once per
row and each sign-in costs about 2.4 seconds, so eight viewers is minutes of legitimate work, and
the probes inside a row already run concurrently.
